title: Gate-in, yard & stowage planning
sceneDesc: The export terminal: a gate with cameras checks the truck and container, then the box is carried into the yard and stacked by a gantry crane. A bay plan shows where it will go on the ship.

narration.1: I pass the terminal [[gate-in|gate]]. Cameras read my number, someone checks my seal and my condition, and I get a receipt.
narration.2: Gate-in: OCR reads container and truck, the pre-advice is matched, seal and damage checked, an [[eir]] is issued. Custody passes to the terminal acting for the carrier. [TO VERIFY:v60]
narration.3: Gate transaction = custody transfer and evidence point: seal, damage, VGM status, DG/OOG/reefer checks. Export detention stops per tariff; storage/demurrage free time starts. [TO VERIFY:v60] [TO VERIFY:v21]

caption.2: From now on, time in the terminal counts against demurrage/storage free time, not detention.

1.reefer: A gantry crane lifts me into the [[yard]]. As a reefer, I'm plugged into electricity so I stay cold.
1.tank: A gantry crane lifts me into a special area for dangerous goods, away from incompatible cargo.
1.oog: I can't be stacked like other boxes, so I wait in a special area for out-of-gauge cargo.
1.*: A gantry crane ([[rtg]]) lifts me into the [[yard]], stacked with other boxes for the same ship.

2.reefer: Reefer rack: plugged in and monitored by the terminal's reefer technicians. [TO VERIFY:v57]
2.tank: DG stack with [[segregation]] per IMDG and port rules; documents checked against the booking. [TO VERIFY:v59]
2.oog: OOG area: no stacking on top, special handling equipment for loading. [TO VERIFY:v58]
2.*: Export stack grouped by vessel, port of discharge and weight class to make loading efficient. [TO VERIFY:v61]

narration.3: Yard planning groups boxes by vessel, POD and weight; reefers on plugs, DG segregated, OOG ungrouped. Dwell beyond free time triggers storage or demurrage. [TO VERIFY:v61]

narration.1: Meanwhile, planners decide exactly where I'll sit on the ship: the [[stowage-plan|stowage plan]]. Heavy boxes low, boxes for the first port on top.
narration.2: Stowage planning uses VGMs, ports of discharge, DG, reefer plugs and stability. The terminal builds the loading sequence from the carrier's plan. [TO VERIFY:v61]
narration.3: Carrier central planner sends the pre-stow; terminal planner sequences moves; final bay plan exchanged as EDI BAPLIE. Only boxes on the load list with VGM and customs release are loaded. [TO VERIFY:v61]
Twelve hours before the vessel arrives, the load list shows your box with status 'CUSTOMS HOLD — documentary check'. The customer hasn't been told.

text.1: The biggest ships on Asia–Europe carry more than 20,000 TEU — and a plan places every single box. [TO VERIFY:v11]
text.2: Every box needs a slot that respects its weight, its port of discharge, DG segregation and reefer plugs — on ships of up to 24,000 TEU. [TO VERIFY:v11] [TO VERIFY:v61]

body.1: At the gate, my number is read by cameras, my seal and my condition are checked, and a receipt is printed. It proves I arrived in good order, on time.

body.2: Export detention stops at full gate-in; terminal storage or demurrage free time starts. Some carriers combine both. [TO VERIFY:v21]
body.3: Long dwell before the vessel (e.g. early gate-in or rollings) can trigger storage charges — check who pays under the contract and the Incoterm. [TO VERIFY:v12]

body.1: A big crane on tyres that stacks containers in the yard.
body.2: RTGs or straddle carriers stack boxes; every extra move ('shifting') costs time, so yard planners avoid digging boxes out. [TO VERIFY:v61]

reefer.1: I'm plugged into electricity so my cooling unit keeps {cargo} at {setPoint}.
reefer.2: Terminal technicians monitor reefers on plugs; temperature records are kept for claims. Plug-in charges may apply. [TO VERIFY:v57]

tank.1: Dangerous goods are kept apart from cargo they could react with.
tank.2: IMDG segregation rules apply in the yard and on board; ports have DG declaration and dwell limits. [TO VERIFY:v59]

oog.1: Nothing can be stacked on me, so I need a special place.
oog.2: Out-of-gauge units take extra slots and special equipment; they are often delivered close to loading. [TO VERIFY:v58]

body.1: Planners place every box on the ship: heavy ones low, boxes for the first port of call on top, special boxes where they're allowed.
body.2: Built from the booking list and VGMs; constraints: stability, lashing forces, port rotation, DG segregation, reefer plugs, OOG slots. Exchanged as EDI BAPLIE. [TO VERIFY:v61]
body.3: Late VGMs or bookings force replanning; overweight or misdeclared boxes can compromise stability and lashing — one reason VGM rules exist. [TO VERIFY:v01]

1.2: The seal is checked against the pre-advice and documents; a mismatch triggers a hold.

2.2: Condition at handover. Damage noted here was there before the terminal took charge — key for claims and repair recharges. [TO VERIFY:v71]

3.2: Some terminals refuse or hold boxes without a VGM at gate-in; all refuse to load them. [TO VERIFY:v01]

2.prompt: What does this gate-in receipt prove?

options.text: When and in what condition the full box was handed over to the terminal
That the box is loaded on the ship
That customs has released the export
options.fb: The release is a separate customs message.
Payment is a commercial matter, not a gate event.

2.explain: The gate-in EIR records time and condition at custody transfer: it stops export detention and anchors any damage claim.

3.prompt: Clean EIR at depot gate-out, but a fresh dent is recorded on this gate-in EIR (merchant haulage). Who is usually charged for the repair?

options.text: The merchant who held the box between the two interchanges

options.fb: The damage was recorded at the terminal's gate, before it took charge.
Possible commercially, but the tariff normally allows a recharge.
Equipment damage follows the equipment interchange terms, not the Incoterm.

3.explain: Two EIRs bracket the period of custody; damage between them is recharged per the carrier's equipment terms. [TO VERIFY:v71]

documents: **Gate-in EIR** — time, seal, condition, VGM status. [TO VERIFY:v60]
**Load list** — boxes cleared for the vessel (VGM, customs, booking).
**Bay plan (BAPLIE)** — where every box goes. [TO VERIFY:v61]

documents.text: **DG manifest** — dangerous goods on board, for the master and ports. [TO VERIFY:v59]

costs: **Origin THC** — terminal handling, per tariff or contract. [TO VERIFY:v35]
**Storage / demurrage** beyond free time in the terminal. [TO VERIFY:v12]

costs.text: **Reefer plug-in / monitoring** charges at some terminals. [TO VERIFY:v57]

costs: **Late-gate fee** if accepted after the cut-off. [TO VERIFY:v12]
risks: **Customs hold** → box can't be loaded; rolled if not released.
**Missing VGM** → not on the load list. [TO VERIFY:v01]
**Damage at gate** → claims and repair recharges.
**Replanning** after late bookings or wrong weights.
jobs: **Terminal operations liaison** — gate issues, holds, load list.
**Vessel / stowage planning** — central planners and terminal planners. [TO VERIFY:v61]
**Customer service** — informing customers of holds and rollings.

incoNote.FCA: Under FCA (terminal), this is the delivery point: risk and cost passed to the buyer on arrival here, ready for unloading. [TO VERIFY:v14]
incoNote.CPT: Under CPT, risk passes on handover to the carrier here, though the seller pays carriage to destination.
incoNote.CIP: Under CIP, risk passes on handover to the carrier here; the seller pays carriage and insurance to destination.
incoNote.FAS: Under FAS, 'alongside' is effectively the terminal for containers — a poor fit; FCA is the right rule. [TO VERIFY:v15]
incoNote.FOB: Under FOB, the seller has lost physical control here but keeps the risk until on board — the classic container gap. [TO VERIFY:v15]

1: At the terminal gate, number, seal and condition are checked and a receipt is issued.
Boxes wait in the yard; reefers are plugged in, dangerous goods are kept apart.
Planners decide where every box goes on the ship.
2: Gate-in = custody transfer and evidence point; export detention stops here (per tariff).
Yard planning groups boxes by vessel, port and weight; special cargo has its own areas.
The stowage plan needs correct VGMs, DG data and reefer details; only cleared boxes load.
3: Holds must be escalated immediately: broker, shipper, customer — before the load list closes.
Two EIRs bracket custody: they decide who pays for damage.
Under FOB/CFR/CIF the seller still carries the risk here — prefer FCA/CPT/CIP for containers.

1.prompt: I'm stacked in the yard and my place on the ship is planned. What happens next?
1.hint: My ship is about to arrive at the quay.

options.text: When my ship arrives, a giant crane loads me on board.
options.confirm: Yes! A quay crane lifts me from a terminal truck onto the ship, following the plan. Under {incoterm}, risk passes to the buyer at step {riskStep}.

options.text: A truck takes me to the customer at destination.
options.why: I haven't crossed the ocean yet!
options.realLife: Delivery happens weeks later, after the voyage and import customs.

options.text: I go back to the shipper to be checked again.
options.why: I was already checked at the gate. Going back would make me miss my ship.
options.realLife: An extra trip, extra costs and a missed sailing.
options.whenRight: Only if the shipper had to fix a real problem (e.g. damaged cargo).

2.prompt: Box in the export yard, VGM received, customs released, stowage planned. What happens next?

options.text: The vessel berths; quay cranes load boxes on the load list in planned sequence; lashing secures them.
options.confirm: Correct. Only boxes on the load list — VGM, customs release, booking — are loaded, in the terminal's crane sequence. [TO VERIFY:v61]

options.text: The shipped-on-board B/L is issued now that the box is in the yard.
options.why: 'Shipped on board' needs the box to be on board.
options.realLife: An early on-board B/L is a false statement.

options.text: The box goes to a CFS for a final check of its contents.
options.why: FCL boxes stay sealed; CFS handling is for LCL.
options.realLife: Opening an FCL box without reason breaks the seal chain.
options.whenRight: Only if customs orders an inspection.

options.text: Boxes are loaded in the order they arrived at the terminal.
options.why: Loading follows the stowage plan, not arrival order.
options.realLife: Random loading would ruin stability and discharge planning.

3.prompt: Case: your box shows 'CUSTOMS HOLD — documentary check' 12 hours before vessel arrival. What do you do?

options.text: Alert the customer and its broker now to supply the documents; track the hold; warn that the box will be rolled if not released before the load list closes.
options.confirm: Right. Only the declarant can clear a customs hold; the carrier's role is fast communication and contingency (rolling). A held box is never loaded. [TO VERIFY:v45]

options.text: Ask the terminal to load it anyway: the hold is only documentary.
options.why: A hold is a hold: terminals don't load held boxes.
options.realLife: Loading would breach customs rules — fines for terminal and carrier.

options.text: Wait: holds are usually lifted automatically.
options.why: Documentary checks need documents from the declarant.
options.realLife: The box misses the vessel and the customer hears it too late.

options.text: Contact customs yourself and send the commercial invoice you have on file.
options.why: The carrier isn't the declarant and may not hold the right documents.
options.realLife: Customs deals with the declarant; unofficial documents can make things worse.
options.whenRight: Only if your company acts as customs broker under a mandate.
